nameStory: The sulphur-winged grasshopper gets its name from the bright yellow hindwings that flash like sulfur powder when it flies. These brilliant wings are normally hidden beneath brown forewings, creating a spectacular surprise when the grasshopper takes to the air. The name 'sulphur' refers to the mineral's characteristic bright yellow color, perfectly matching this grasshopper's wing display.
description: The sulphur-winged grasshopper is a medium-sized grasshopper with cryptic brown and gray coloring on its body and forewings that helps it blend into the ground. When disturbed, it reveals stunning bright yellow hindwings bordered with black as it flies in short, erratic bursts. These grasshoppers are part of the short-horned grasshopper family, meaning their antennae are relatively short compared to their body length. Adults typically measure about an inch to an inch and a half in length.

idTips.label: Bright yellow hindwings
idTips.description: When the grasshopper flies or is handled, brilliant sulfur-yellow hindwings with dark borders flash into view - they're impossible to miss once revealed

idTips.label: Mottled brown forewings
idTips.description: At rest, the forewings appear dusty brown and gray with darker mottling, feeling papery to the touch and perfectly camouflaging the insect against soil and dead leaves

idTips.label: Short, thick antennae
idTips.description: The antennae are noticeably shorter than the body length and feel firm when gently touched, distinguishing it from long-horned grasshoppers and katydids

idTips.label: Crackling flight sound
idTips.description: Makes a distinctive crackling or rattling sound when flying, created by the wings hitting together - you'll often hear it before you see the yellow wings

idTips.label: Ground-hugging behavior
idTips.description: Tends to stay close to bare ground and flies in short, low bursts before landing and immediately folding its colorful wings out of sight

habitat: Look for sulphur-winged grasshoppers in open, sunny areas with patches of bare or sparse soil, including old fields, meadow edges, hiking trails, and disturbed ground. They prefer areas with some exposed earth mixed with low vegetation, often found along forest edges where sunlight creates warm microclimates. In New England, they're common in abandoned pastures, power line corridors, and rocky outcrops from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring and are most active on warm, sunny days. This is when they're called 'spring yellow-winged grasshoppers' and are easiest to spot as they seek mates.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in early to mid-summer when adults are fully developed and most numerous. Listen for their crackling flight sounds and watch for yellow wing flashes in open areas.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall but become less common as temperatures drop. Late season individuals may appear more worn with faded coloring.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - they overwinter as eggs in the soil, completely hidden from view until the next spring's emergence.

funFact: Sulphur-winged grasshoppers are nature's magicians - they can completely vanish the instant they land by tucking their brilliant yellow wings under drab forewings, transforming from a flash of sunshine into an invisible speck of dirt in less than a second.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative, the autumn yellow-winged grasshopper, which has similar bright yellow hindwings but appears later in the season (hence 'autumn' vs 'spring'). Memory trick: if you see yellow-winged grasshoppers before mid-summer, they're likely the spring species (sulphur-winged).
contextualKnowledge: The terms 'grasshopper' and 'locust' are often used interchangeably for the same insects - this species is sometimes called the 'spring yellow-winged locust.' True locusts are simply grasshoppers that form destructive swarms under certain conditions, though New England species rarely exhibit this swarming behavior.
compareHints: The sulphur-winged grasshopper differs from its closest relative, the autumn yellow-winged grasshopper, primarily in timing - sulphur-winged adults are active from late spring through mid-summer, while autumn yellow-winged adults peak in late summer and fall. Both have similar bright yellow hindwings, but the seasonal separation makes identification straightforward if you note when you observe them.
